section.title: Preparing to Cross the Jordan
section.sectionRationale: God's charge to Joshua now becomes action. Joshua issues his first orders as leader: the whole camp is to prepare provisions to cross the Jordan within three days, and the eastern tribes, who already have their land, are reminded of their pledge to fight alongside their brothers until all Israel has rest. The people answer with wholehearted obedience and their own echo of God's charge, be strong and courageous. It is one movement, the mobilizing of a united people for the promise ahead.
section.thesis: The rest God gives is a shared rest: the tribes already settled must not enjoy their inheritance while their brothers are still without theirs, and the united, obedient response of the people, echoing back the very words God spoke to Joshua, shows Israel taking up the promise together under God's word.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the order to prepare provisions to cross within three days, verses 10 to 11; the reminder to the eastern tribes of their pledge to help until all have rest, verses 12 to 15; and the people's wholehearted answer of obedience and courage, verses 16 to 18.

units.label: The order to prepare to cross
units.note: within three days you will cross the Jordan

verses.text: Then Joshua commanded the officers of the people:

“Go through the camp and tell the people, ‘Prepare your provisions, for within three days you will cross the Jordan to go in and take {{yarash|possession}} of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.’”

units.label: The eastern tribes reminded of their pledge
units.note: until the LORD gives your brothers rest

verses.text: But to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joshua said,
“Remember what Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you when he said, ‘The LORD your God will give you {{menuchah|rest}}, and He will give you this land.’

Your wives, your young children, and your livestock may remain in the land that Moses gave you on this side of the Jordan. But all your mighty men of valor must be armed for battle to cross over ahead of your brothers and help them,

until the LORD gives them rest as He has done for you, and your brothers also possess the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you may return to the land of your {{nachalah|inheritance}} and take possession of that which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you on the east side of the Jordan.”

units.label: The people's wholehearted answer
units.note: all you command us we will do; be strong and courageous

verses.text: So they answered Joshua, “Everything you have commanded us we will do, and everywhere you send us we will go.
Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. And may the LORD your God be with you, as He was with Moses.
Anyone who rebels against your order and does not obey your words, all that you command him, will be put to death. Above all, be {{chazaq|strong}} and courageous!”

yarash.gloss: To take possession of, to dispossess, to inherit. This is one of the key verbs of Joshua: Israel is to go in and take possession of the land the LORD is giving. It holds together two truths that run through the whole book, the land is God's gift, and yet it must be actively taken hold of; grace given is grace to be entered by faith and obedience.

menuchah.gloss: Rest, a settled resting place, security. The LORD's gift to His people is menuchah, a home where the wandering and warfare cease. In Joshua rest means secure settlement in the land; the New Testament shows this earthly rest to be a shadow of the deeper Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God in Christ, Hebrews 4:9.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, allotted possession, heritage. The land each tribe receives is its nachalah, a portion handed down by promise rather than seized by right. The eastern tribes already hold their inheritance east of the Jordan, yet they must help win their brothers' inheritance before returning to enjoy their own.

chazaq.gloss: To be strong, firm, resolute. The very command God pressed on Joshua, be strong, the people now speak back to him, be strong and courageous. Their obedience is not grudging but eager, taking up God's own word and returning it to their leader as encouragement.

basic.context: God has commissioned Joshua; now Joshua acts. His first order as leader is practical: get ready, because in three days we cross the Jordan into the land God is giving us. Then he turns to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, who had already received land on the east side of the Jordan. They had promised Moses they would send their fighting men across to help the other tribes conquer their land before settling down themselves. Joshua holds them to it: no one rests until everyone rests. The people respond with striking unity, promising full obedience and echoing God's own charge back to Joshua, be strong and courageous. The question underneath is: what does it look like for God's people to take up His promise together?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing how Israel mobilized. The specific arrangement with the eastern tribes belongs to that moment, and the harsh penalty for rebellion reflects Israel's covenant life under Moses' law, not a rule for the church. What endures is the pattern: God's people obey His word, act on His promise, and refuse to enjoy their own blessing while their brothers still lack theirs. The rest sought here also points beyond itself to a greater rest.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel is to go in and yarash, take possession of, the land God gives, a verb that holds grace and effort together. God's gift is menuchah, rest, a settled home. Each tribe's portion is its nachalah, its inheritance. And the people answer Joshua by echoing God's word to him: be chazaq, be strong.
basic.typology: The eastern tribes crossing over to fight for their brothers' rest before enjoying their own pictures the way God's people are bound together, not resting alone but laboring for one another's inheritance. The rest of the land points forward to the true rest in Christ. Joshua leading a united people foreshadows Christ gathering one people into one inheritance.
basic.christ: The rest Israel seeks in the land is a shadow of the rest Jesus gives: Come to Me, all you who are weary, and I will give you rest, Matthew 11:28. And the solidarity of the tribes, none resting while others lack, reflects the body of Christ, where members care for one another and no one is meant to arrive at the inheritance alone.
basic.god: God is the giver of rest and land; every step forward rests on what the LORD your God is giving you. He is the God who keeps His people together in one purpose, and who is worthy of the wholehearted obedience the people pledge. The whole scene assumes that God's promise is sure, so that preparation and courage are simply the fitting response to His faithfulness.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 32 records the original pledge of the eastern tribes to Moses. Deuteronomy 3 repeats Moses' charge to them. Hebrews 4 shows that Israel's rest in the land was a shadow of the greater rest in Christ. And Galatians 6 calls believers to bear one another's burdens, echoing the tribes' shared labor.
basic.oneStory: The promise of land moves from God's charge to Joshua into the united action of the whole people. Israel prepares to cross, the settled tribes take up their brothers' cause, and all pledge obedience. It is another step in God bringing His people into their inheritance, and the rest they seek points ahead to the lasting rest Jesus gives.

context.literary:
The passage completes the commissioning of verses 1-9 by showing it acted on immediately; Joshua does not pause to reflect before verse 10, he commands. The unit is arranged in three matched speeches, Joshua to the officers, verses 10-11; Joshua to the eastern tribes, verses 12-15; and the people's answer to Joshua, verses 16-18, each carrying its own weight, as though the passage itself is quickening pace toward the crossing.

A structural echo binds the whole chapter together. The final words the people speak to Joshua, be strong and courageous, verse 18, are the identical words God had just spoken to Joshua in verses 6, 7, and 9, so that the divine charge to one man becomes, within the same chapter, the whole nation's charge back to him, an inclusio that turns private commissioning into public, shared resolve.

The unit is also built on a deliberate contrast in address. Joshua speaks to the officers with bare command, prepare your provisions; he speaks to the eastern tribes with a reminder wrapped in memory, remember what Moses commanded you; and the people answer him with a pledge that itself echoes their earlier obedience to Moses, just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you, so the passage traces continuity of leadership through three different registers of speech in the space of nine verses.
context.historical:
The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh had asked Moses for the well watered grazing land of Gilead and Bashan on the Jordan's east side because their livestock, described in Numbers 32:1 as very great, needed exactly that kind of terrain; Moses granted the request only after securing a binding military pledge, recorded in full in Numbers 32:20-32, that their fighting men would cross over armed and would not return to their own land until the rest of Israel's inheritance was won.

Three days was a realistic but urgent window; the Jordan valley near Jericho lies well below sea level, and the river at this time of year, close to the spring harvest and the original Passover season, would be swollen with snowmelt from the northern highlands, at flood stage rather than at its usual shallow crossing depth, a detail the narrative itself notes once the crossing actually happens, Joshua 3:15. Provisions needed gathering now because the miraculous daily supply of manna, which had fed Israel without any need for stockpiling for forty years, was due to stop almost as soon as Israel ate from the produce of the land itself, Joshua 5:11-12.

The death penalty threatened in verse 18 for open rebellion against Joshua's command reflects the severity ancient Israel's covenant law attached to organized defiance of a divinely appointed leader, comparable to the treatment of a rebellious son in Deuteronomy 21:18-21 or open contempt of a judge in Deuteronomy 17:12.
context.canonical:
This scene answers a promise made a generation earlier. Numbers 32:20-24 recorded the eastern tribes' own conditional vow, if you will arm yourselves for battle before the LORD and cross the Jordan, and warned them plainly, if you do not, you will have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out; Joshua's reminder here holds that exact vow open and unresolved until it is finally honored in full, Joshua 22:1-4, once the western conquest is complete.

The chapter's repeated language of rest ties the eastern tribes' settled inheritance to the whole Torah's larger vocabulary of Sabbath and promised rest, stretching back to creation's own seventh day, Genesis 2:2-3, and forward through Deuteronomy 12:9-10's promise that Israel had not yet entered the rest and the inheritance the LORD was giving.

The people's pledge, everything you have commanded us we will do, deliberately answers Israel's earlier covenant promise to Moses at Sinai, all that the LORD has spoken we will do, Exodus 19:8 and 24:3, showing the narrator wants readers to hear this generation renewing, almost word for word, a vow their parents once made and later broke.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The writer wants to show a leadership transition succeeding where it easily could have failed. A newly commissioned leader could have hesitated, and a tribe already granted its own land could have quietly withdrawn from a war that no longer touched their own borders; the author records neither happening, Joshua acts without delay and the eastern tribes are held, without apparent resistance, to a promise made a generation earlier. The intent is to demonstrate covenant loyalty operating on two fronts at once, vertical obedience to God's charge and horizontal obligation between tribes, so that readers see a single command, be strong and courageous, translating immediately into both individual resolve and communal solidarity. The author also wants the reader to notice whose words the people finally speak back to Joshua, since their closing pledge repeats God's own charge, showing that the whole nation, not only its leader, has now taken hold of the same word.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The specific military arrangement, which tribes must cross armed and which families may remain behind, and the death penalty attached to rebellion, describe Israel's own covenant law in a particular moment of national mobilization and are not instructions transferable to church discipline today. What the passage does model as an enduring pattern is the refusal to let a settled portion of God's people rest comfortably while others still labor for their own inheritance, together with a whole community's wholehearted, undelayed response to a leader's word, everything you have commanded us we will do, and everywhere you send us we will go, a pledge the New Testament expects believers to embody toward Christ rather than toward any single human leader.

debates.question: Was it right for the eastern tribes to settle east of the Jordan, outside the land promised to Abraham?

views.label: A legitimate arrangement honored by God
views.case: Moses granted the request under a binding condition, Numbers 32, and here Joshua and God's narrative treat their inheritance as valid; the land east of the Jordan was among the territories God gave Israel to possess, and the tribes faithfully keep their word by crossing to fight.

views.label: A concession that carried later risk
views.case: Their choice, driven partly by their large herds, placed them on the far side of the Jordan from the heart of the nation and its worship, and later chapters show the tension this could create, Joshua 22; some read it as a permitted but spiritually precarious decision.

debates.bearing: Either way, the passage stresses their obligation to the whole, whatever the wisdom of settling east, they must not enjoy their rest while their brothers remain unsettled, a picture of shared responsibility among God's people.

debates.question: Does the harsh penalty the people attach to their own pledge in verse 18 undercut the wholehearted obedience the verse otherwise describes?

views.label: A standard covenant sanction, not a sign of coercion
views.case: Capital penalties for organized rebellion against a divinely appointed leader appear elsewhere in Israel's law, Deuteronomy 17:12, and the tone throughout verses 16-18 is eager rather than reluctant, everything you have commanded us we will do coming before, not after, the penalty is even mentioned.

views.label: A hint that unity here is more aspiration than accomplished fact
views.case: The very next major narrative episodes, Achan's hidden sin in chapter 7 and the near civil war over an altar in chapter 22, show that Israel's unity and obedience were nothing like automatic, so some readers hear the harshness of verse 18 as the narrator's own quiet acknowledgment that wholehearted unity would need constant, costly enforcement rather than arriving naturally.

debates.bearing: The text presents the ideal, a nation speaking with one voice, without pretending the ideal was ever easy to keep; readers are meant to admire the pledge and, a few chapters later, to notice honestly how quickly it was tested.

study.originalLanguages:
Joshua's first order, verse 11, tells the people to ready provisions, a Hebrew word that elsewhere names the supplies a traveler packs for a journey, as when Jacob's sons carry provisions down to Egypt, Genesis 42:25, and shares a root with the very food Isaac asks Esau to hunt before his blessing, Genesis 27:3. The word quietly recalls two earlier journeys, exile into Egypt and a father's blessing given under pressure of time, both now folded into Israel's own urgent three day preparation to leave the wilderness behind.

Twice the chapter calls the eastern tribes' soldiers mighty men of valor, verse 14, a fixed military title used later of Gideon, Judges 6:12, and of Boaz, a man of standing, Ruth 2:1, marking not mere numbers but a recognized class of seasoned, capable fighters, so their crossing is no token gesture but the commitment of Israel's actual strength to a war that will not touch their own land again.

The verb that governs the whole chapter is cross over, used of the Jordan itself, verses 11 and 14, and repeated so often through the rest of the book that some scholars connect it to Israel's very name for itself in Genesis, Hebrew, one who crosses over, first used of Abraham after his own crossing into Canaan, Genesis 14:13; if the connection holds, Israel's identity was bound up with river crossings long before this one.

And the penalty in verse 18, all that you command him will be put to death, uses a fixed legal formula, surely he shall be put to death, the same doubled construction that marks the gravest capital laws throughout the Torah, Exodus 21:12 and Leviticus 24:16, showing the people are not speaking loosely but binding their pledge to the full weight of covenant law's own language for the most serious offenses. Even the officers Joshua addresses in verse 10 carry a title, literally scribes or writers, an administrative class attested throughout the Torah for organizing the camp, Exodus 5:6, Deuteronomy 20:5, so the very first word of action in this chapter runs through Israel's ordinary chain of command rather than a fresh miracle, the extraordinary crossing about to come is prepared for by entirely ordinary, unglamorous bureaucracy, the same kind of unnamed, faithful service Scripture quietly assumes behind almost every great deliverance it records.

typology.type: The eastern tribes crossing over to fight for their brothers' rest before returning to enjoy their own, verses 12-15
typology.fulfillment: Their fighting men leave a genuinely good inheritance temporarily unenjoyed for the sake of others who have nothing yet; Paul's picture of the body of Christ works the same way, where no member can say to another I have no need of you, 1 Corinthians 12:21, and Galatians 6:2 turns the same principle into a direct command, bear one another's burdens. The type escalates from a temporary military obligation between related tribes to a permanent, spiritual solidarity binding believers who may share no bloodline at all.

typology.type: The rest promised through Moses and now near for the eastern tribes, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: Rest here still means a settled, secure home free from war, a real but limited good that later history would take away again. Jesus offers rest to the weary on far broader terms, come to me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest, Matthew 11:28, a rest of the soul rather than of the land, which is why Hebrews can still call it a Sabbath rest that remains, unclaimed by any conquest, for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9.

typology.type: The people's pledge, everything you have commanded us we will do, spoken back to a newly commissioned leader, verses 16-17
typology.fulfillment: Israel's promise here proved fragile within a single generation of Joshua's own death, Judges 2:10-11. The greater Joshua receives a different kind of pledge, one his Spirit keeps rather than merely records, since Ezekiel had already looked forward to a day when God would put his own Spirit in his people so that they would keep his statutes, Ezekiel 36:26-27, a promise fulfilled at Pentecost rather than merely spoken and later broken.

study.christ:
The great word carried through this passage is rest, verse 13, the settled home Moses had promised the eastern tribes and that Joshua now moves the whole nation to secure. Israel's rest here is real and geographical, yet it is also partial from the very start, granted to only two and a half tribes while the other nine and a half still had to fight, and granted, even for the eastern tribes themselves, only after further war on someone else's behalf. Rest that must still be worked for and shared before it can be enjoyed is already a rest that points beyond itself.

Jesus takes up the very word when he calls the weary and burdened to himself, promising a rest that requires no further war to earn and no further waiting for a brother's inheritance to be settled before it can be enjoyed, Matthew 11:28-29. Hebrews draws the historical line explicitly, since Joshua's own generation still fell through unbelief, and since David long after Joshua kept urging Israel toward a rest called today, a further Sabbath rest must remain for God's people, one Joshua's conquest, real as it was, could never supply, Hebrews 4:6-9.

The unity commanded here, no tribe resting while its brothers still lack, also anticipates the shape of the church Christ forms, one body drawn from many members who cannot treat each other's needs as someone else's problem, Ephesians 4:4-6 and 1 Corinthians 12:26, so that the very structure of shared labor for a shared rest, first modeled by armed men crossing a river for tribes not their own, becomes the ordinary pattern of how Christ's people are meant to carry one another toward an inheritance none of them could secure alone. Even the officers who carry Joshua's word to the camp in verse 10 model something of this pattern in miniature, ordinary appointed servants relaying a leader's command so that the whole people can move together, a small picture of how the risen Christ's own commission is carried by ordinary messengers to the ends of the earth, Acts 1:8.
study.god:
Every step in this passage rests on a possessive pronoun repeated until it becomes almost a refrain, the land that the LORD your God is giving you, verse 11, this land that Moses gave you, verse 14, and the land that the LORD your God is giving them, verse 15. Three times in five verses ownership is assigned to God before it is assigned to any tribe, so that the entire military campaign about to begin is framed, before a single sword is drawn, as receiving a gift rather than winning a prize.

God is also shown holding a whole nation to a promise across a full generation. Nothing in this chapter suggests the eastern tribes' vow to Moses had lapsed simply because Moses had died; Joshua enforces an obligation sworn to a leader now gone, on behalf of a God whose memory of a promise does not weaken with time or with a change in leadership. That continuity is itself a claim about God's own faithfulness, since a covenant kept alive across a change of human leaders reflects a covenant Keeper who does not change.

He is, finally, the God whose own earlier word to Joshua becomes contagious. The people's closing pledge borrows God's own vocabulary, be strong and courageous, back to their leader, so that the command first spoken privately by God to one man is, by the chapter's end, circulating through an entire nation as its own settled resolve; a single word from God, taken seriously, does not stay confined to the person who first received it. For worship, the passage teaches that shared obedience, and shared rest, both begin in a gift God gives before anyone has done anything to deserve it. He is, too, a God who works through the most unremarkable channels available, officers repeating a command through the camp, families managing herds and children left behind, so that the miracle waiting at the Jordan is preceded by nothing more dramatic than careful, obedient logistics, a reminder that God's greatest acts are usually prepared for in very ordinary ways.

crossReferences.note: The eastern tribes' own conditional vow to Moses, arm yourselves for battle before the LORD and cross the Jordan until your brothers are settled, or else your sin will find you out, is the exact promise Joshua now holds them to, showing this scene as the overdue fulfillment of a bargain struck a full generation earlier.

Only after the western conquest is finished does Joshua release the eastern tribes to return home, telling them plainly that they have kept every word Moses commanded them, the narrative's own confirmation, chapters later, that the pledge made here in chapter one was actually honored in full.

Israel's answer to Joshua, everything you have commanded us we will do, echoes almost word for word the nation's earlier vow at Sinai, all that the LORD has spoken we will do, inviting the reader to notice how much weight now rests on this generation keeping a promise its parents did not.

Moses had already told Israel they had not yet come to the rest and the inheritance the LORD was giving, a rest still future when he spoke it and still future here, showing how long this particular promise had been carried forward before Joshua could finally act on it.

Jesus offers weary people the very rest Israel's land could only picture in geography, a rest for the soul rather than a ceasefire from war, available the moment anyone comes to him rather than after further battles fought on someone else's behalf.

Because the appeal to enter God's rest kept being repeated long after Joshua's campaign ended, the writer concludes that a further Sabbath rest still remains for God's people, proof that even a successful, obedient conquest like this one was never the final word on rest.

Paul's picture of one body with many members, unable to say to each other I have no need of you, gives the New Testament's fullest statement of the very principle enacted here, that no part of God's people rests easy while another part still lacks.

Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ, turns the eastern tribes' one-time military obligation into a standing command for every believer, making shared labor for another's good an ordinary feature of Christian life rather than an unusual exception.

study.oneStory:
The promise of land, sworn to Abraham and renewed to Moses, has just been spoken again over Joshua in verses 1-9; this passage shows that promise beginning to move through an entire nation's feet rather than staying words spoken to one leader. Provisions are packed, an old debt between tribes is called in, and a whole people answers with language borrowed from their own parents' worst broken vow at Sinai, everything you have commanded us we will do, daring to repeat a promise their parents once made and then failed to keep.

The chapter's insistence that no tribe rest while others still lack theirs becomes, across the rest of Scripture, one of the clearest pictures of what it looks like for God's people to carry a shared inheritance rather than a collection of private ones. It anticipates the New Testament's vision of one body, many members, one Lord, one faith, Ephesians 4:4-6, long before there was a church to embody it.

And the rest this generation moves toward, real, geographical, and hard won, still leaves later Scripture unsatisfied, since Hebrews insists a further rest remains even after Joshua's own conquest succeeded. The passage therefore sits at a hopeful but unfinished point in the larger story, a nation acting in unity on God's ancient promise, and still, centuries later, waiting, as every reader still waits, for the greater Joshua who alone can lead all of God's people into a rest that never has to be shared out unevenly or defended by anyone's sword again. Even the officers and the quiet arrangements of these verses matter to that larger story, since the God who will part a river in the next chapter is the same God content to work through provisions gathered, promises kept, and orders passed down an ordinary chain of command.

quiz.q: What was Joshua's first command to the people as their new leader?

options.text: Prepare provisions, because within three days they would cross the Jordan to take the land.
options.note: Verses 10 to 11 record this as Joshua's opening order through the officers.

options.text: Assemble at the tabernacle to renew the covenant first.
options.note: Covenant renewal comes later in Joshua; his first command here is to prepare to cross within three days.
Spies are sent in chapter 2, but Joshua's first recorded command is to prepare provisions to cross.

options.text: Wait a full month for the Jordan floodwaters to fall.
options.note: He commands crossing within three days, while the river is at flood, not waiting for it to subside.

quiz.q: Why did Joshua remind the eastern tribes of their pledge?

options.text: Their fighting men must cross over to help until all the tribes had rest, before returning to their own land.
options.note: Verses 12 to 15 hold them to the pledge made to Moses in Numbers 32.

options.text: They were to give up their eastern land entirely and settle in Canaan.
options.note: They kept their eastern inheritance; the pledge was to fight for their brothers first, not to abandon their land.

options.text: They had to pay the other tribes for the land they held.
options.note: No payment is involved; the obligation was to share in the fighting until all had rest.

options.text: They were being punished for choosing land east of the Jordan.
options.note: This is not punishment; Joshua holds them to a promise they had freely made.

quiz.q: What principle governs the tribes' shared inheritance?

options.text: No tribe should enjoy its rest while other tribes still lack theirs.
options.note: The eastern tribes must help win their brothers' land before returning to their own, verses 14 to 15.

options.text: Each tribe should look after its own inheritance and leave the others to theirs.
options.note: The opposite: the settled tribes are bound to labor for the others, not to keep to themselves.

options.text: The strongest tribes deserve the largest share.
options.note: Allotment is by God's assignment, not strength; the point here is shared labor for a shared rest.

options.text: Only the tribes who crossed the Jordan matter to God.
options.note: The eastern tribes are fully included; the concern is that all Israel share the rest together.

quiz.q: How did the people respond to Joshua's leadership?

options.text: With wholehearted obedience, pledging to do all he commanded and echoing God's charge, be strong and courageous.
options.note: Verses 16 to 18 show their eager, united response and their echo of God's word to Joshua.

options.text: They obeyed but complained about the danger of the flooded Jordan.
options.note: They did obey, but the text records eager commitment, not complaint, unlike the wilderness generation.

options.text: They demanded that Joshua first prove himself in battle.
options.note: They asked for no proof; they pledged obedience and prayed God would be with him as with Moses.

options.text: They refused until Joshua reduced the workload.
options.note: There is no refusal; they promise full obedience, everything you have commanded us we will do.

questions: The settled tribes were called to fight for their brothers before enjoying their own rest. Where might God be calling you to labor for someone else's good rather than settling into your own comfort?
The people pledged, everything you have commanded us we will do, and everywhere you send us we will go. Is there an area where your obedience to God is partial rather than wholehearted?
Israel had to prepare and act on a promise that was still ahead of them. What promise of God are you being called to move toward in faith right now?
The rest Israel sought in the land points to the deeper rest Jesus gives. Where are you weary, and what would it mean to bring that weariness to Christ for His rest?
The people encouraged Joshua with the very words God had spoken to him. Who in your life needs you to speak God's word back to them as encouragement this week?

translationNotes.note: Mighty men of valor renders a Hebrew phrase for able-bodied warriors; the eastern tribes' soldiers, not their whole population, were to cross and fight.
Rest here renders menuchah, a settled resting place; the same theme of God-given rest runs from Deuteronomy through to Hebrews 4.
The penalty of death for rebellion reflects Israel's covenant law under Moses in a unique historical moment and is not a rule carried over to the church.
